title: Not the whole life at once
word: Not the whole life at once
hook: don't let the picture of your whole life crush you; take this piece (Meditations 8.36)

segments.voice: Yesterday: one action at a time, a life built the way you'd build a wall, stone by stone. Your line was one action at a time. Which action did you do well? Day six hundred two, the end of a week.

It's Sunday night and you open the calendar. Not this week. The whole year. The lease renewal, the move, the parent who's getting older, the money that has to stretch until spring. In thirty seconds every trouble you might ever have is sitting on your chest at once. None of it is happening yet. All of it feels heavy. Marcus Aurelius knew that weight. He ruled through years of war and plague, and a few entries after yesterday's, he wrote himself a short note about exactly this feeling. Today: not the whole life at once.
screen: `THE WHOLE YEAR ON YOUR CHEST.` → `NONE OF IT HAPPENING YET.` → `NOT THE WHOLE LIFE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: First, the note. In book eight Marcus tells himself not to let his thoughts gather up, all at once, every hardship he expects to meet. George Long's 1862 translation begins it plainly: “Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life.” Second, the question. Instead, Marcus says, with each thing as it arrives, ask: what in this is actually unbearable, past bearing? He thinks you'd be embarrassed to answer. Most present moments, looked at alone, are smaller than the dread that came with them. Third, the shrinking trick. Neither the past nor the future weighs on you, he writes, only the present. And even the present gets smaller if you mark it off by itself, draw its edges tight around this hour, and then ask your mind whether it really can't hold out against something so little. Fourth, why it isn't avoidance. Marcus planned campaigns and wrote laws; he didn't stop thinking ahead. The note is about carrying, not planning. You can plan the year on paper and still carry only today. And the week, looking back: not by reputation, steadily, no blaming, fig, what it means, one action at a time, and now, this piece only. Book eight keeps making the same move. It shrinks the field until what's left is something a person can actually do.
screen: `DON'T PICTURE THE WHOLE LIFE.` · `ASK: WHAT HERE IS UNBEARABLE?` · `MARK THE PRESENT OFF BY ITSELF.` · `PLAN THE YEAR, CARRY THE DAY.` · then, large: `THIS PIECE ONLY.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the big picture come up for a moment: the year, the list, the worries. Notice its weight. Now draw a small box around today. Just today. What actually has to happen between now and sleep? Name two or three things, no more. Anything outside the box, set it on a shelf. It will still be there tomorrow, and tomorrow it gets its own box. Breathe with only today's box in view. The bell holds the time.
Not the whole life at once. Marcus's note to himself: don't carry every expected trouble together; take the present piece, and ask what in it is truly unbearable. Today's word.
screen: `NOT THE WHOLE LIFE AT ONCE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: this piece only. Plan only today. When tomorrow's worry shows up, say this piece only, and come back to the box. Day six hundred two.

howItsDone: Many people who read the Meditations keep a list for today rather than a worry list for the year, and when dread about the future rises they ask Marcus's question of the present hour: what here is actually unbearable?

original.note: Greek: the present, what is at hand. Marcus wrote the Meditations in Greek.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't think about the future.
what it means: plan if you need to, but carry only the present piece, and ask what in it is truly unbearable.
what a scholar hears: Marcus wrote these notes in Greek, to himself; the heading in the manuscripts, ta eis heauton, means roughly to himself, and may not be his own.

sources.quoted: Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life.

notes: Confirm the exact wording of Long's 8.36 opening: 'Do not disturb thyself by thinking of the whole of thy life.'

8.36 paraphrase: don't gather all expected troubles; ask of each 'what is there in this which is intolerable'; neither past nor future pains you, only the present, which is diminished if circumscribed. Confirm.
